history.summary: CSV TOWN ERROR: 'Nongpoh' is wrong — the temple is at Nartiang in the West Jaintia Hills district (Nartiang was the summer capital of the Jaintia Kingdom; do not conflate with any Nongpoh shrine). CSV 'state' column wrongly holds the town name; the real state is MEGHALAYA. A royal Shakti shrine of the Jaintia kings and one of the 51 Shakti Peethas, where Sati Devi's left thigh is believed to have fallen. Legend says King Dhan Manik (1596-1612) made Nartiang his summer capital, and that Goddess Durga appeared in a dream — attributed variously to Dhan Manik or to King Jaso Manik (1606-1641), whose Hindu queen Lakshmi Narayana, daughter of Koch king Nara Narayana, is said to have influenced the royal house toward Shakti worship. Built on a hilltop above the Myntang river in Khasi-house style (central dieng blai pillar, thatch, later tin roof); the basement holds the 'Boli Garbha' sacrificial pier. Priests are descendants of the Deshmukh family invited from the west centuries ago. Vintage Jaintia cannons stand in the complex. Human sacrifice in earlier times was replaced by goat sacrifice (sources conflict on dates; flag). Exact construction date unverified — flag.

name: Nartiang Durga Temple
town_description: Nartiang is a historic village in the West Jaintia Hills district, about 65 km from Shillong, once the summer capital of the Jaintia Kingdom. It is famous for the Nartiang monoliths — tall stone pillars, the tallest about 27 feet, called the 'Stonehenge of the North East' — and for its ancient Durga and Shiva temples.

travel.road: About 65 km from Shillong by road via Jowai; Nartiang market is the nearest landmark
